Dog Care Guide

How to take great care of a dog

A dog depends on you for everything: food, safety, exercise, health and love. Here is what every dog needs to live a happy, healthy life.

Food and water

  • Feed a good dog food made for your dog's age and size (puppy, adult or senior).
  • Puppies eat 3 to 4 small meals a day. Most adult dogs eat 2 meals a day.
  • Measure the food so your dog doesn't get overweight.
  • Always keep fresh, clean water out.
  • Treats are fine, but only a small part of what they eat each day.

Foods that are poisonous to dogs

  • Chocolate (dark chocolate is the worst)
  • Grapes and raisins, which can hurt their kidneys
  • Onions and garlic
  • Xylitol, a sweetener in sugar-free gum, candy and some peanut butter
  • Macadamia nuts, alcohol and caffeine
  • Cooked bones, which can splinter

If your dog eats one of these, call a vet right away.

Exercise and play

  • Every dog needs a walk or playtime every day. Young and high-energy breeds need more.
  • Games like fetch, tug and puzzle toys keep their brain busy too.
  • A bored dog may chew, dig or bark a lot. Exercise helps.
  • On hot days, put the back of your hand on the pavement. If it is too hot for you, it is too hot for their paws.

Vet care

  • Visit the vet for a checkup at least once a year.
  • Keep up with vaccines like rabies, distemper and parvo.
  • Use flea, tick and heartworm prevention.
  • Spaying or neutering helps stop unwanted puppies.
  • Call a vet if your dog stops eating, keeps throwing up, has trouble breathing or seems very tired.

Grooming and teeth

  • Brush their fur often. Long-haired dogs need it almost every day.
  • Trim their nails so they don't get too long.
  • Brush their teeth with dog toothpaste only. Human toothpaste can make them sick.
  • Give a bath when they are dirty, and check their ears and paws.

Training and kindness

  • Reward good behavior with treats, praise and play.
  • Never hit or yell at a dog. It makes them scared, not good.
  • Use the same words and rules every time so your dog learns fast.
  • Let puppies meet lots of people, sounds and friendly dogs so they grow up confident.

Safety

  • Your dog should wear an ID tag and have a microchip in case they get lost.
  • Use a leash near roads.
  • Never leave a dog in a hot car, not even for a few minutes. Cars get dangerously hot very fast.
  • Keep medicine, cleaning products and trash where your dog can't reach them.

Love and company

  • Dogs are pack animals. They get lonely and sad when left alone all day.
  • Give them a soft bed, toys and a quiet place to rest.
  • Spend time with them every day: cuddles, walks and games.
  • A dog can live 10 to 15 years or more. Getting one is a promise for their whole life.

Learn the truth

Puppy mills: why they are so bad

A puppy mill is a dog breeding business that cares about making money, not about the dogs. Dogs are kept in crowded, dirty cages and bred over and over so the owners can sell as many puppies as possible.

Life inside a puppy mill

  • Dogs live in small wire cages, often stacked on top of each other.
  • Many never get to walk on grass, play or go for a walk.
  • Cages are often dirty, too hot in summer and too cold in winter.
  • They get very little or no vet care, grooming or love.

The mother dogs

  • Mother dogs are bred again and again, with almost no rest in between.
  • They often spend their whole lives in a cage.
  • When they can't have puppies anymore, many are thrown away, sold off or worse.

The puppies

  • Puppies are often taken from their mom too young.
  • Many are sick with things like parvo, kennel cough or worms when they are sold.
  • Careless breeding can cause problems they are born with, like bad hips or heart problems.
  • Because they never met people or other dogs, many grow up scared or anxious.

Where the puppies end up

  • Many pet stores that sell puppies get them from puppy mills.
  • Websites and online ads with cute photos that ship puppies to you.
  • Flea markets, parking lots and roadside sales.
  • A seller saying "licensed breeder" doesn't prove the dogs are treated well.
Red flags: signs a seller may be a puppy mill
  • They won't let you visit or see where the dogs live.
  • You can't meet the puppy's mom.
  • They want to meet in a parking lot or ship the puppy without you ever seeing it.
  • They always have lots of puppies, often many different breeds.
  • They want to sell a puppy younger than 8 weeks old.
  • They have no vet records, or they don't ask you any questions about your home.
How you can help stop puppy mills

Adopt, don't shop

  • Adopt from an animal shelter or rescue. They have puppies, grown dogs and even purebreds.
  • Every adopted dog is a life saved and one less dollar for puppy mills.
  • Shelter dogs usually already have vaccines and are spayed or neutered.

If your family buys a puppy

  • Only buy from a responsible breeder you can visit in person.
  • Meet the mom and see that the dogs are clean, healthy and happy.
  • A good breeder asks you lots of questions and will take the dog back if needed.
  • Don't buy puppies from pet stores or from ads that ship puppies sight unseen.

Spread the word

Tell your friends and family about puppy mills. Many people buy from pet stores or online without knowing where the puppies came from. Some cities and states have already made laws stopping pet stores from selling puppy mill dogs. When fewer people buy these puppies, fewer dogs have to suffer.

Quick check: true or false?

A puppy from a pet store is always from a good, caring breeder.

False. Many pet store puppies come from puppy mills.

You should be able to meet a puppy's mom before getting the puppy.

True. A good breeder is happy to show you the mom and where the dogs live.

Chocolate is a safe treat for dogs.

False. Chocolate is poisonous to dogs.

Shelters and rescues have puppies and even purebred dogs.

True. Adopting is a great way to find a dog and fight puppy mills.

Health & Routine

Essential Dog Care Pillars

Hydration & Health

Ensure dogs have access to fresh water daily. Active pups require extra fluids after exercise.

Coat & Grooming

Regular brushing prevents matting, distributes natural coat oils, and reduces shedding.

Mental Stimulation

Use puzzle toys and scent tracking games to prevent boredom and reduce anxiety.

Dental Care

Brush teeth using dog-safe toothpaste or provide veterinary-approved dental chews.
